md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass the flag `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which also moves pages that other processes share, and so needs CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux capability: one of the slices of root privilege a process can hold). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, the Linux asynchronous I/O interface built on shared submission and completion rings; SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: A density map gives a number, not a list of objects. You cannot crop, identify or follow an individual from it, and the count is real-valued. Use it when objects are too dense to box, not as a default.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
md: chroot changes how paths are looked up, nothing more. Open file descriptors, the working directory and root's privileges all ignore it. Real filesystem isolation needs a mount namespace, no privilege to undo it, and no handles that point outside.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Requirements and collection plans: decide before you search
md: No requirement, no collection. A plan that names sources, legal basis and retention keeps an investigation focused, defensible and small.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: Geolocate places and events, not private people. Working out where a private individual lives or goes from their photos is stalking, whatever the technique is called. Practise on public landmarks, games built for it, or published case studies.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: Never practise on real private people, including friends who "don't mind". Use public landmarks, fictional scenarios, practice platforms, and your own organisation with written permission.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Sparse data: how a few ratings re-identified Netflix users
md: In sparse, high-dimensional data, every person is an outlier. A handful of rare facts, even noisy ones, is enough to find a record, and then the whole record is exposed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Never let users re-run a noisy query for free. Repeated noisy answers can be averaged; composition counts every one. Cache answers or charge each run to the budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
md: Do not treat LINDDUN as a compliance checklist. Its value is the same as STRIDE's: asking each element and flow "how could this hurt the people in the data?" before the design is fixed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise
md: A privacy review asks, in order: what data actions happen, how they could hurt people (LINDDUN), whether the processing is necessary (DPIA), what must leave the system and the matching technique (DP, PSI, secure aggregation, or not releasing), how the design minimises, and how rights reach every copy.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021: about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Linux runs, on each CPU, a task that has not had more than its weighted fair share: CFS picks the smallest vruntime; EEVDF picks, among eligible tasks (lag of zero or more), the earliest virtual deadline. Nice values set weights 1.25x apart; slices end on ticks and wakeups, and those are your involuntary switches.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them
md: Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: Misconception: "we validate all input, so we are safe". Format checks (is it an integer, is it a known product) do not test meaning (is this quantity possible, is this step allowed now, has this coupon been used). Logic flaws live in the meaning.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Starbucks gift cards and two browser sessions (2015)
md: Protect the resource being spent, not the path to it. A one-time flag in the session, a disabled button or a cleared form all guard one route to the balance; a lock or atomic update on the balance itself guards every route.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: Write the invariant first, then a test that tries to break it in every way this course showed: odd values, odd order, and many at once. A test suite with no parallel test cannot fail on a race.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
md: Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
md: Joining hypervisors, backup servers and RMM consoles to the production domain feels tidy, but it gives whoever owns AD the keys to everything at once. Separate authentication for these systems is the single design choice that most often decides whether a domain compromise becomes a business-ending outage.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
md: Every reward-side fix encodes an assumption about *where* the reward is wrong: in members' disagreement, in label noise, in a named feature, or in extreme values. Hacks that live outside that assumption pass straight through, so these methods complement an outside check; they do not replace it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` (results skipped plus the page length) exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Placement is decided when a task lands in a local DSQ. `select_cpu` and the idle cpumask choose where, `LOCAL_ON` puts it there from any CPU, and kicks (`IDLE`, `PREEMPT`) decide when that CPU looks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Secrets: what they are, how long they live, why they sprawl
md: A secret's danger is what it opens, times how long it works, times how many places it lives. Every technique in this course shrinks one of those three: least privilege shrinks the first, rotation and dynamic secrets the second, vaults and scanning the third.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets
md: The best secret is one that does not exist at rest. Where one must exist, make it short-lived, unique to one consumer, held in one audited place and rotated automatically with overlap.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Any code that writes `obj[key] = value` with a key from input, or walks nested input recursively, must refuse `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, or use objects with no prototype. Any string that reaches eval, Function or a string timer is code injection.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand
md: Warnings find bugs; hardening flags limit the damage of the bugs you missed. Review build files like code: a change that removes either, or adds -Wno-format-security or -fno-stack-protector, needs the same scrutiny as a change to authentication.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
md: A common misconception: tunnel mode is not more encrypted than transport mode. Both use the same ESP encryption. Tunnel mode additionally hides the inner addresses and lets a gateway protect traffic for a whole network; transport mode is for two hosts protecting their own traffic.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Encrypting email itself: S/MIME, OpenPGP and EFAIL (2018)
md: EFAIL's root cause was releasing unauthenticated plaintext into an active renderer (HTML that fetches URLs). Authenticated encryption plus a strict rule (verify first, show nothing on failure) removes the gadget attack; disabling remote content in the client removes the easiest exfiltration channel.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
md: In an access-proxy design the device inventory and the identity system are part of the trusted computing base. If the inventory says a stolen laptop is healthy, every check downstream agrees.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
md: A security automation is a small distributed system that holds powerful credentials and processes data attackers can influence. Design for duplicates, partial failure and hostile input from the first version.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Measuring AI triage: golden sets, precision, recall and attack success
md: Golden-set labels must come from completed investigations. If you label with first-look verdicts, you measure how well the model copies hurried humans, including their misses.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
md: Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access. Insiders already have access. The defence emphasis differs for each, but removing unused access helps against all of them.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Kill chain: seven phases, and breaking any link stops the intrusion. ATT&CK: tactics (why) and techniques (how) with IDs, the shared language of detection rules and threat reports.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Building a programme from zero: the first 90 days
md: Inventory and owners first, then cheap actions that remove whole classes of risk, then a written strategy and budget built on what you found. Tools come after you know what they will watch and who will respond.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Reporting to the board: oversight duties and the annual cycle
md: A board is not an operations audience. Pages of vulnerability counts, tool names or "attacks blocked" give directors nothing to oversee and can later read as a CISO who never explained the real risk. Equally, never let the pack say something rosier than the internal record (lesson 15).

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Rebuilding after failure: Equifax, Maersk and Microsoft
md: Rebuilds that last change who leads and to whom they report, what leaders are rewarded for, how often the board looks, and what the company says publicly, not only how much it spends.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
md: Do not present fear or vanity. Breach headlines from other companies and "millions of attacks blocked" both waste the board's attention. Directors respond to clear risk, honest measures and a specific ask, and they remember who was straight with them.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
md: Turning off DTDs (DOCTYPE declarations) removes the whole feature: no DTD, no entity declarations, so no external entity fetch and no billion laughs. OWASP's first rule is to disable DTDs whenever possible, and to keep XInclude off too, since it loads documents without any DTD. If a format truly needs DTDs, disable external entities and external DTD loading explicitly, and keep the parser library up to date.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
md: Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
md: Do not ask people to detect lies in real time. Give them a rule that does not depend on the caller being honest, and make following the rule faster than arguing.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
md: The people layer is defended by design (processes that do not depend on spotting lies), by technology that makes mistakes harmless, and by a culture where reporting is fast, safe and thanked. Blame breaks all three.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
md: A latent's name comes from what it reads (activating examples across the whole activation range, plus its density) and what it writes (its logit effect). Automated pipelines write names with one LLM and score them with another by simulation, detection or fuzzing; all of these are correlational, so finish with a causal check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation, which holds out whole regions so test points are not right next to training points) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: A log-mel spectrogram is 80 numbers every 10 ms. Whisper's 30 second input is therefore an 80 x 3000 matrix: the model never sees raw samples.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
md: A process is one sparse virtual address space: a handful of VMAs (code, data, bss, heap, mappings, libraries, stack, vdso), each with its own permissions and backing, separated by vast unmapped gaps, at addresses ASLR moves on every run.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: what erasing the refusal direction reveals
md: The guarantee is narrow. It covers linear classifiers, the activations whose means you computed, and the population those means stand for. A nonlinear probe may still recover the concept, a direction estimated on one split or layer is only approximately right on another, and refusal ablation applies one layer's direction at every layer, where it is not that layer's mean difference.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: Teacher forcing is a training trick. At inference the decoder only ever sees its own earlier outputs, mistakes included, and the encoder output is computed once per source sentence, not once per step.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
md: BM25 = sum over query terms of IDF x f / (f + k1 x (1 - b + b x |d| / avgdl)). Three statistics per term and document: f, |d|, and n_t; two per collection: N and avgdl.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: A density value is not a probability, so it can be larger than 1. A density squeezed onto a narrow range must be tall to keep its total area at 1: spread evenly over an interval of width 0.5, its height is 2. Only areas under a density are probabilities.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
md: The Hessian holds the curvature in every direction. Its eigenvalues classify a critical point (all positive: minimum; mixed signs: saddle), the largest one sets the stable learning rate $2/\lambda_{\max}$, and their ratio sets how slowly gradient descent converges.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: Inside `[ ]`, quote every variable: `[ "$x" = foo ]`. An empty or spaced value otherwise changes how many arguments `[` receives, and the test fails with an error instead of returning false. Inside `[[ ]]` a variable needs no quotes, except on the right of `==` or `=~`: there quotes make the pattern literal, so `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file named `*.log`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
md: Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: Compile each `.c` file separately into a `.o`, then link them. The preprocessor pastes text, the compiler checks one translation unit at a time, and the linker joins units together by symbol name.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Narrow types promote to int before arithmetic; mixed signed and unsigned operands usually become unsigned; conversion to unsigned wraps modulo 2 to the width. Compile with `-Wall -Wextra` and read every sign warning.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Check every return value from a library call. On failure, errno says why; perror and strerror turn it into text. Release resources on every path, typically through one cleanup label, and report the outcome through the exit status.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: A lifetime parameter on a struct marks it as a view into data it does not own, and the checker keeps every use of the view inside the data's lifetime. Return `&'a T` from a method to tie the result to the data rather than to the struct.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches
md: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$: eigenvectors are the directions $A$ only stretches, eigenvalues the stretch factors, found from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. Repeated multiplication is dominated by the largest $|\lambda|$. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors: $S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
md: Gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L$. On a quadratic, each step multiplies the error by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per direction, so it converges only if $\eta < 2/\lambda$ for every curvature $\lambda$, and the sharpest direction sets the limit.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: Expected test error = bias squared + variance + noise. Simple models miss systematically (bias), flexible models chase noise (variance), and the noise sets a floor nobody can beat. Regularization and more data mainly cut variance.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
md: A complete training loop is: split, fit preprocessing on train, shuffle each epoch, step on minibatch gradients plus the penalty gradient, watch validation loss, keep the best weights, and evaluate on test once. Every bug in later, bigger models is a violation of one of these steps.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form
md: A batched gradient is the per-example gradient summed (or averaged) over the rows of the batch. The transposes are just how a matrix product writes that sum, and a quick check that every gradient has the shape of its parameter catches most mistakes.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
md: No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: Most concurrency bugs are atomicity violations (fix: a lock around the whole check-then-act) or order violations (fix: a condition variable on a state variable). Deadlock needs four conditions; the usual cure is to acquire locks in one global order.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: The mean answers "total divided by count", the median answers "what is typical", and tail percentiles answer "how bad is it for the unlucky few". For skewed data, report more than the mean.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: The CDF turns any range question into a subtraction, $F(b) - F(a)$. Standardizing turns any normal question into the standard normal CDF, $\Phi$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 3), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size (here the 2 point gap) and its confidence interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler, which never puts the same text twice in one batch, for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: Initialization is about **variance, not values**. Pick the weight scale so that each layer multiplies the activation variance (and the gradient variance) by about 1. For ReLU that means $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/\text{fan-in}$; with depth, any other factor compounds exponentially.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
md: Every stage is a trust boundary, and attackers pick the stage with the widest fan-out: one poisoned library, build server or CI action reaches thousands of victims at once. Defence means asking, for each arrow, what proves the thing arriving is the thing you expected.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
md: Provenance moves the question from 'do I trust this file?' to 'do I trust this repository, this workflow and this build platform?', which you can check by machine. npm's documentation is explicit that provenance does not guarantee a package has no malicious code; it makes origin verifiable.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: To share writable memory, both processes need `MAP_SHARED` mappings of the same pages: anonymous before `fork`, a `shm_open` name, or a memfd descriptor. Then order the accesses with release and acquire atomics or a lock; the mapping itself guarantees no ordering at all.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Tree search for reasoning: Tree of Thoughts, MCTS, inference laws
md: Tree search pays when you have a step-level evaluator you can trust (code that runs, a checked answer, a strong PRM) and when early mistakes are expensive, as in Game of 24. With a weak evaluator, more search mostly finds the evaluator's mistakes, the over-optimization seen in lesson 5. And always compare at equal compute: rollouts are not free.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent (one gradient step per token, in arrival order) on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong through false sharing.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
md: LOTL hunts are baseline hunts in disguise. The tools are legitimate, so the evidence is never the tool alone: it is the tool used by an account, on a host, at a time, or in a sequence that this environment has not seen before.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
md: Do not average the two grades into one number, and do not let the letter drive the digit. "A5" (a reliable source passing on something improbable) is a perfectly valid and useful grade: it tells the reader to check before acting, whoever sent it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Writing an intelligence product people act on
md: A good intelligence product states a judgement, says how likely and how sure in standard words, shows the evidence and its grade, tells each reader what to do and by when, admits its gaps, and asks for feedback. Everything else in CTI exists to make that page right.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
md: Default deny, check every request in one place, keep that place small, and assume the attacker has read the code. Most broken access control bugs violate at least one of these four.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: The padlock icon means "this connection is encrypted to the named site", not "this site is safe". Phishing sites get valid certificates for their own domains in seconds.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
md: mTLS answers "which service is calling?". It does not answer "is this service allowed to do this?". Authorization (orders may charge, but not refund) is still your application's job, keyed on the verified identity.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, which give a process its own view of process ids, mounts and network, and cgroups, control groups that cap its CPU, memory and I/O). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: Remember the condition that makes resharding free: choose generation groups so that **each GPU's generation shard contains its training shard**. Then the only traffic is one all-gather per micro DP group, and no GPU keeps a second copy.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
md: Generating a frame is not one forward pass. Each frame costs a full MaskGIT loop (25 passes in Genie) over a context that grows with every frame. The paper's own limitations: Genie runs at around 1 FPS and is limited to 16 frames of memory.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
